title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
hook: eyes, nose, mouth, tongue, skin: the classical morning wakes the senses one by one

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine, dinacharya, began before sunrise: rise in brahma muhurta to protect life, and ask the body first. Who got tomorrow's first minute? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-five.

Lay the classical texts' morning care side by side and it covers a lot of ground in a small space: a tour of the face, eyes, nose, teeth, tongue and mouth, and then the skin, all of it. Read quickly, it's a hygiene checklist. Read slowly, it's something else: a way of waking the senses up one at a time, so the person who walks out the door has actually arrived in their own body. It's the last day of the week, too, so we'll look back before we look in. Today: the senses, one by one.
screen: `EYES, NOSE, TEETH, TONGUE.` → `A TOUR OF THE FACE.` → `THE SENSES, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The Charaka Samhita and the Ashtanga Hridaya both walk through this morning care, in their own order. Paraphrased: the eyes are tended. The teeth are cleaned with a twig, chewed into a soft brush. The tongue is scraped. The mouth is rinsed and gargled, sometimes with oil. Drops of oil may go in the nose. Then oil for the body, and a bath. Each of these is a door. The eyes see, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the skin feels. And in Hindu thought the senses matter far beyond hygiene. The Gita, for one, pictures a steady person drawing the senses in, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs. The morning round doesn't preach about any of that. It just touches each door, gently, before the day starts knocking on all of them. Notice the order, too: from the head down, from small to whole. A twig for the teeth before oil for the whole body. That's a kind of attention you can feel. Not hurried. Not skipped because nobody's watching. Now, the week we've walked. The doshas took their turns on the clock, stacked like on like, split into nature and today, and closed on health as the three in balance. Then we opened the daily round: dina, day, charya, conduct. We rose before sunrise, in the verse at least, to protect life, and checked in with the body first. And today the senses, woken one by one. The thread through all of it is the same. Ayurveda keeps building health out of ordinary minutes.
screen: `EYES, TEETH, TONGUE, MOUTH, SKIN` · `EACH SENSE IS A DOOR` · `FROM THE HEAD DOWN, SMALL TO WHOLE` · `THE WEEK: ORDINARY MINUTES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wake each sense, without moving. Stay just as you are. Start with the eyes: soften them, notice light and shape. Then the ears: the nearest sound, then the farthest. The nose: the air, any smell at all. The tongue: resting, the taste of the mouth right now. Then the skin: clothes, air, the weight where you sit. Door by door. Then let them all rest together in the breath. If you pray, you can name each sense as a gift as you pass it. The bell holds the time.
The daily routine. In the classical morning, eyes, teeth, tongue, mouth and skin are each tended in turn, waking the senses one by one. Today's word.

Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. Tomorrow at the sink, give each step its own moment: the eyes, the teeth, the tongue, the face, as if you were waking them in turn. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda's morning round tend the eyes, clean the teeth, scrape the tongue, rinse or gargle the mouth, and some use oil in the nose or on the body before bathing.

original.note: Sanskrit indriya: a sense, or sense faculty, in Ayurveda and in the Upanishads and the Gita.

trapdoor: what you thought: morning care is a hygiene checklist.
what it means: the daily round tends each sense, eyes, teeth, tongue, mouth, skin, waking the person into the body.
what a scholar hears: indriya, the senses, a word Ayurveda shares with the Upanishads and the Gita, where the senses are gathered in.

sources.ref: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 5 (morning care: eyes, nasal oil, tooth twig, tongue scraper, gargling, oil, bath)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2 (dinacharya: tooth twig, eye care, nasal drops, gargling, oil massage, bath)
Bhagavad Gita 2.58 (the one who withdraws the senses from their objects, as a tortoise draws in its limbs)
